Subject: Streaming bottleneck diagnostics — discovery recap & next steps

Hi Aisha — thanks again for the time today. Quick recap from our discovery so we have alignment and clear next steps. Please reply with any corrections.

Summary of pain & goals
- Pain: end-users experience jitter and partial token delivery during streaming responses; spikes in perceived latency during peak traffic.
- Business impact: checkout assistant timeouts on mobile leading to abandoned carts during promos (~$60k monthly impact).
- Short-term goal: reduce user-visible p95 of token-delivery to <250ms for streaming sessions and flatten jitter across tokens.
- Long-term: support 150–300 concurrent conversational sessions with stable tail latency, and a predictable cost per 1K tokens.

What you shared about current stack
- In-house inference on K8s with mixed G4/G5 nodes; model is an open transformer quantized to 8-bit.
- Prefetching + sticky sessions via session cookie; no KV cache shared across pods today.
- Observed p95 ~450ms with peaks up to 1.2s under load. Typical request length ~120–160 tokens.

Key technical diagnostic hypotheses (for prioritization)
1) KV/cache misses & cross-pod cold-starts for streaming sessions causing early-token spikes.
2) Small-batch scheduling on GPU leading to kernel launch overhead at low concurrency.
3) Network copy / socket flush frequency affecting chunked-token delivery and perceived jitter.

Success criteria (agreed-ish)
- p95 token delivery <250ms across representative requests (measured in-staging).
- Streaming chunk jitter reduced by >40% (client-observed standard deviation).
- Autoscaler behavior that avoids full cold-starts for interactive sessions.

Immediate next steps (owners & timing)
- Marcus (me): run an initial pass of the sample trace you shared and provide a short diagnostics summary — ETA: EOD Monday (2026-11-02). Attachment: sample_trace_20261029.json.
- FastRetail (Aisha/Rajiv): confirm peak concurrency windows and attach a short anonymized kube node inventory + current HPA rules — ETA: EOD Friday (2026-10-31).
- Jordan: propose a micro-checklist (kernel profile, prefix-caching toggle, batch size sweep) that we can run in your staging — ETA: Mon morning (2026-11-02).
- Book a technical deep-dive with infra + SRE (45 min) to run through traces and tuning. Marcus to propose times in a follow-up.

Attachments: sample_trace_20261029.json (json), config_snapshot_20261029.tar.gz (tgz).

If that all looks right, I’ll schedule the deep-dive and bring a short demo of our trace annotations and streaming-quality view.

Thanks,
Marcus Lin

Thanks Marcus — that recap is accurate. A few clarifications and extra context below.

Current infra details we can share now
- Nodes: mix of AWS G4dn.xlarge + a handful of G5 instances for hot workers.
- Orchestration: K8s 1.26, custom HPA (CPU + queue-length based) that scales from 4 -> 40 pods during peaks.
- Average request: 1 prompt + dynamic context (~120–160 tokens). 2nd-turn prompts shorter (~40–80 tokens).
- Observed metrics: p95 token latency ~450ms, cold session first-token sometimes >1s; streaming chunk sizes configured by our frontend at 8 tokens per chunk.

What we can provide today (attached / forthcoming)
- sample_trace_20261029.json (attached) — sanitized traces from two peak windows (10/28 14:00–15:00 and 10/29 19:00–20:00).
- config_snapshot_20261029.tar.gz — includes HPA rules and pod resource requests.

Questions for Redwood
- How disruptive is enabling a shared KV cache across pods? Any special infra requirements?
- Can you demonstrate how streaming chunk flush frequency maps to perceived jitter? We’re worried tuning chunk size will hurt token-level latency.

We can do a deep-dive next week. Rajiv (SRE) will join and wants to see proposed kernel/batching experiments. Friday 11/05 or Monday 11/08 are best for us.

Aisha
Sr. Platform Engineer, FastRetail

Thanks Aisha — useful details. Quick technical checklist we typically run to isolate the three hypotheses Marcus listed:

1) KV/prefix cache validation
- Confirm whether session affinity is causing cache fragmentation (cookie -> pod mapping). If yes, try a read-only shared KV (Redis/Redis-compatible) in staging to observe miss-rate changes.

2) Batch/kernel overhead sweep
- Run a micro-benchmark that varies batch sizes (1, 2, 4, 8) for your typical 120-token requests. Look at mean kernel launch time and per-token delta.

3) Network flush & chunk sizing
- Temporarily instrument the frontend to emit per-chunk send timestamps, and correlate with backend token flush intervals.

Concrete proposal for the deep-dive (45 min)
- 10 min: walk through the sample traces with Marcus — highlight token-level tail events.
- 20 min: run a live trace annotation session (we can replay a sanitized trace in our console).
- 15 min: agree on 2 experiments to run in staging (KV shared test, batch-size sweep).

I’ve dropped a short perf profile link that shows how we annotate per-kernel costs — will send privately in the calendar invite.

Would Friday 11/05 10:30–11:15 PT work for you and Rajiv? Marcus / Lauren can join.

—Jordan
